summary: A discussion of the print file type in the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol, written before an FTP meeting. It reviews how vertical format control for printed output should be treated, and how the Remote Job Entry protocol seemed to force one particular interpretation. It updates RFC 354, 385 and 454.

plainLanguage.summary: Some files are meant to be printed on paper, with page breaks and line spacing. People disagreed about how to handle those when sending files.

questions: ftp type a e i l
subtitle: Why FTP's print file type was confusing, and two ways to reconcile it with the Remote Job Entry protocol.

tldr.problem: Contributors to FTP and RJE were unhappy with the print file type, and FTP offered only two cases while printer processes use three ways to handle vertical format control.
tldr.mechanism: R. Braden describes three cases (N, T and A), shows how RJE maps them onto FTP format and structure attributes, and lays out two choices for fixing the mismatch.
tldr.outcome: Either make record structure the FTP default so that unformatted, unstructured files become print files, or add three formats to FTP matching Cases N, A and T.

today: RFC 448 is a 1973 discussion paper that, per its header, updates RFC 354, RFC 385 and RFC 454. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown, and the text does not say which choice was adopted.

sections.title: The Print File Problem
sections.content:
Many of those who helped define FTP and RJE expressed uncertainty or unhappiness with the "print file" type in FTP. This RFC reviews the problem ahead of the forthcoming FTP meeting. It was first drafted from RFC 385 and updated to the terminology of the latest FTP document, RFC 454.

It also notes that the Network RJE protocol as defined seems to force a particular interpretation of print files in FTP, probably different from the one most FTP implementors assumed.
sections.plainLanguage: People disagreed about what a "file for printing" really is, and this note sorts out why.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Vertical Format Control
sections.content:
A print file is one intended for a printer process and containing vertical format control (VFC) information, such as single or double spacing, overprinting and page ejection. There are three common ways printer processes determine VFC, using RJE's labels:

  • Case N, non-print file: no VFC information, and the printer applies a standard format.
  • Case T, ASCII format effectors: a Telnet-like file using CR, LF and FF.
  • Case A, ASA (Fortran) VFC: the first character of each record is a VFC code.

RFC 454 seems to provide only two FTP cases, unformatted and print file, and it is unclear how they relate to the three. Tenex supports only Case T, while IBM operating systems support Cases N and A, so a server must decide whether a stored file gets the internal print file attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: A page can have no layout notes, layout notes written as ordinary line breaks, or a special code at the start of every line. FTP only had room for two of those three ideas.

sections.title: What RJE Implies and the Two Choices
sections.content:
To send an output file to a user host, the RJE server has the user's FTP process send it as: Case N, Unformatted with Record structure; Case T, Unformatted with File structure; Case A, Print File with Record structure. So RJE uses the structure attribute to tell Cases N and T apart.

For perfect consistency, an FTP server using ASA VFC internally would convert every (Unformatted, Unstructured) file it receives into an internal print file, which implies the default file structure in FTP should become record structure. The other choice is to change FTP to include three formats corresponding to Cases N, A and T, with RJE changed to match.
sections.plainLanguage: One fix changes the everyday default to match the printing system. The other adds a third option so nothing has to be forced.
